turns.text:
Absolutely, I'd be happy to help clarify! Sigmund Freud and Jacques Lacan are both influential figures in psychology, particularly in the area of psychoanalysis.

Freud proposed the Oedipus complex, a theory suggesting that during a critical stage in childhood, children may develop feelings of attraction towards the opposite-sex parent while feeling jealousy and anger towards the same-sex parent. He saw this as a crucial step in personality development.

Lacan, building on Freud's work, argued that the Oedipus complex isn't just a personal struggle but also a reflection of societal norms and expectations. In other words, children learn to conform to societal rules not only through punishment and reward but also by internalizing these norms as they navigate their Oedipal phase.

So, in a nutshell, the Oedipus complex isn't just about personal desires; it's also about how individuals adopt and internalize societal expectations, which can shape their desires and behaviors. This idea is particularly relevant when discussing cultural influences on individual identity and behavior.
